planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in spring once frost danger has passed, in well-drained soil; mulch roots in cold winters to protect against hard freezes.

directions: This compact New Zealand shrub carries glossy, purple-tinged bronze-green foliage year-round and produces spikes of violet-blue flowers from midsummer into autumn, often continuing later than most other hebes. Grow it in gritty, sharply drained soil, since soggy roots in winter are the most common cause of failure. Shear back lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and to prevent the woody, leggy growth hebes can develop with age. It combines well in mixed borders or containers and tolerates coastal wind and salt spray.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

common_name: Red Edge Hebe (Grey-Green Foliage with Crimson Margins)

planting.note: Plant in spring in free-draining soil; the foliage color develops best with plenty of direct sun, and cold snaps often deepen the red margin.

directions: Prized mainly for its foliage rather than its short lilac flower spikes, this small mounding hebe carries narrow grey-green leaves edged in a thin band of red that intensifies with cool temperatures and bright light. It stays neat and low without pruning, making it a reliable choice for edging paths or filling gaps at the front of a border. Give it gritty, well-drained soil and avoid winter wet, which is far more damaging to hebes than cold alone. Established plants handle short dry spells and coastal exposure without complaint.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, well-drained soil; this is one of the hardiest and most reliable hebes for cooler climates and tolerates light shade.

directions: One of the most widely planted groundcover hebes, this low, spreading selection forms a tight mat of small, rounded, blue-grey leaves that hold their color through winter. Clusters of small white flowers appear in early summer but are secondary to the foliage effect. It roots easily from cuttings, spreads steadily without becoming invasive, and works well spilling over walls, in rockeries, or as underplanting at the front of shrub borders. It is notably more cold-tolerant and shade-tolerant than most larger-leaved hebes.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

common_name: Emerald Gem Hebe (Dwarf Dense Mounding Shrub)

planting.note: Plant in spring in sharply drained soil; its very tight, slow-growing habit makes it well suited to troughs, rockeries, and containers.

directions: This dwarf hebe forms an exceptionally dense, tidy dome of small, tightly packed dark green leaves and rarely needs pruning to keep its shape. Small white flowers appear occasionally in summer but the plant is grown chiefly for its neat evergreen structure rather than bloom. Its slow growth rate and compact size suit rock gardens, edging, and mixed containers where a low, unfussy evergreen accent is wanted. Like other hebes it resents wet feet, so plant in gritty, free-draining soil and avoid heavy clay.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist but well-drained soil; this larger species tolerates more shade and damper ground than most compact hebes.

directions: Known in New Zealand as koromiko, this fast-growing species has long, narrow, willow-like leaves and produces slender racemes of white to pale lilac flowers over a long summer season. It grows considerably larger and more open than most cultivated hebes and can be pruned hard in spring to keep it shapely. It tolerates damper soil and more shade than compact rockery hebes, making it useful as an informal screen or background shrub at a woodland edge. Young growth is attractive to browsing deer and rabbits in some regions.

planting.note: Plant in spring after frost danger passes, in fertile, well-drained soil; this species is one of the least cold-tolerant hebes and needs winter protection outside mild coastal climates.

directions: Native to exposed coastal cliffs of the North Island, this is one of the showiest hebe species, with broad, glossy dark green leaves and dense spikes of magenta-purple flowers that can appear intermittently much of the year in mild climates. It is more tender than most cultivated hebes and performs best in coastal gardens with mild winters, since hard frost damages both foliage and stems. Its parentage runs through many of the large-flowered garden hebe hybrids sold today. Give it full sun, fertile soil, and shelter from harsh drying wind for the best floral display.

planting.note: Plant in spring in gritty, well-drained soil; this small-leaved species is among the more cold-hardy hebes and tolerates light shade.

directions: This tidy, rounded species carries small, thick, blue-grey leaves densely packed on stiff stems, giving the whole plant a cool silvery cast even without flowers. Short spikes of white flowers open in early summer and are a modest bonus to the foliage display. It stays compact and symmetrical with minimal pruning, making it useful for the front of a border, low hedging, or rock gardens. Like most small-leaved hebes it prefers lean, sharply drained soil and resents winter waterlogging.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; deadhead spent flower spikes to prolong the long summer-to-autumn bloom season.

directions: Named for the Welsh headland where it originated as a chance seedling, this popular garden hebe produces tapering spikes of bright pink flowers that fade to paler pink as they age, giving a two-tone effect over a bloom season that can run from midsummer well into fall. Its glossy mid-green leaves and rounded habit make it a dependable structural shrub even when not in flower. It performs best in full sun with sharply drained soil and benefits from a light trim after flowering to maintain density. It is one of the more widely available and reliable border hebes in cultivation.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Space plants for a low hedge in spring in well-drained soil; trim after flowering to maintain a neat, naturally rounded form.

directions: Named for the Rakaia River gorge in New Zealand's South Island, this species forms a naturally dense, tidy dome of bright apple-green foliage even without clipping, which has made it one of the most widely planted low hedging hebes. Small white flowers appear in early summer but are secondary to its foliage value. It tolerates regular trimming far better than most hebes, holding a formal shape well, while also thriving left informal as a mounding specimen. It is among the hardier hebe species and handles both coastal exposure and inland cold better than many showier cultivars.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil; its scale-like foliage and upright habit make it a useful substitute for dwarf conifers in small gardens.

directions: Among the most distinctive hebes in cultivation, this species belongs to the 'whipcord' group whose leaves are reduced to tiny overlapping scales pressed tight against slender stems, giving the whole plant the texture and silhouette of a small cypress or juniper rather than a typical broadleaf shrub. Pale lavender flowers appear in small clusters in summer but are easy to overlook against the fine grey-green foliage. It grows slowly into an upright, airy mound and needs little pruning to maintain its naturally elegant form. Well-drained soil is essential, as it is more prone to root rot in heavy or waterlogged ground than broader-leaved hebes.
